newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian politician aims to revive euthanasia.
newsitem.headline: Australian politician aims to revive euthanasia.

text.p: An Australian politician on Wednesday began an attempt to revive euthanasia in the Northern Territory by ammending laws to carry only a minor fine for helping a terminally ill person die.
Last month the Australian national parliament overturned the Northern Territory's voluntary euthanasia law -- the world's only assisted suicide law.

Northern Territory politician John Bailey on Tuesday introduced legislation into the local parliament which, if passed, would result in doctors who helped terminally ill patients die being fined A$50 (US$39).
"The (legislation) I am proposing...creates an offence called euthanasia," Bailey told Reuters by telephone from Darwin, capital of the Northern Territory.
"If a person admits to it, he or she will be given an infringement notice and fined A$50 but no conviction will be recorded," Bailey said.
Four people used the territory's euthanasia law during its nine month existance, using a computer-controlled machine that injected a lethal drug.
A terminally ill woman, who gained the medical signatures necessary to use the euthanasia law but failed to act before it was overturned, died last week after a coma induced by drugs.
The territory's euthanasia law was overturned despite 75 percent of Australians backing voluntary euthanasia for the terminally ill.
Bailey's bill aims at amending the Rights of The Terminally Ill Act, which remains on the Northern Territory statute books despite being overturned by the national parliament.

Bailey said he hoped to gather support for his bill from territory politicians who had opposed the original euthanasia law but who were now angry about perceived interference by the national government in the territory's affairs.
Australia's national parliament can overturn laws in the country's two territories but not its six states.
Bailey's bill will not be debated until August.
